name: Houttuynia cordata
lead: Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint, heartleaf or chameleon plant, is a perennial native to Southeast Asia used as a vegetable and herb in Vietnam, Japan, Korea, northeastern India and southwestern China, and in traditional Chinese medicine.[1] Its extract, marketed as "heartleaf", is a prominent ingredient in Korean skincare toners, serums and sheet masks, where brands position it for calming redness, balancing oil and clearing the look of congested pores.[1][2]

People use it for appearance in two ways: topically through K-beauty products aimed at blemish-prone or reactive skin, and as a traditional tea. The route people describe is calmer skin inflammation and less oil leading to a clearer, more even-looking complexion. Review articles describe anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies [8][9][10].

Evidence on skin is mostly laboratory-based; Wikipedia notes there was no high-quality clinical research confirming safety or effectiveness as of 2018.[1] Injectable preparations have caused severe allergic reactions.[1]

paras: The plant grows in moist shady places, spreads by rhizomes and is considered invasive. Its leaves have a fishy taste from the volatile compound decanoyl acetaldehyde.[1] In China it is used for conditions such as pneumonia, abscesses and skin infections in traditional medicine; in Korean folk medicine for colds.[2]

The plant grows 0.6 to 1 metre tall with heart-shaped leaves and white-bracted flower spikes, favouring moist, shady sites. It regrows from rhizome fragments, which makes it invasive in gardens, and it is naturalised in North America [1].

As food, northeast Indian cooks use leaves in salads and chutneys; Vietnamese cuisine serves the leaves (diep ca) with grilled meat and noodle dishes; Japanese and Korean traditions drink it as dried-leaf tea; and in southwestern China the rhizome and leaves are eaten, for example in cold salads and dipping sauces [1]. The leaf's fishy taste and smell come from the volatile oil decanoyl acetaldehyde [1].

Brands cite antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, with extract typically at 1 to 3 percent in products marketed for redness, pores, sebum and hydration, popular in K-beauty since the 2010s.[1][2] Cell studies report flavonoids such as quercitrin reducing inflammatory mediators and antibacterial activity against Cutibacterium acnes; a small toner study is reported to show reduced sebum and improved moisture at 8 weeks, with few design details available.[2]

Reviews report that the plant contains volatile oils, alkaloids, flavonoids and phenolic acids, with flavonoids and volatile oils named as the main active components [8]. Review authors describe laboratory and animal findings on organ protection, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiviral and antibacterial effects [8][9][10]. A 2018 review concentrates on inflammation and oxidative stress [5]. These studies mostly use extracts or isolated compounds in cells or animals rather than finished skincare products.

Laboratory studies and reviews have examined anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antiviral activities of the plant, including activity against influenza and herpes simplex virus in cell systems.[3][4][5] A review of anti-inflammatory and oxidative-stress effects was published in 2018.[5]

Patch testing before topical use is suggested in one source because of reported contact dermatitis in sensitive users.[2] In a rat 28-day study high oral doses caused liver and kidney toxicity, and China suspended intravenous use of herbal injections in 2006 after severe reactions including anaphylaxis.[2] Aristolactam components have raised kidney-cell toxicity concerns in vitro.[2]

No controlled clinical trials of Houttuynia cordata for skin appearance were found in the registries and literature reviewed. Registered trials of products containing it address respiratory infection, dry eye and atopic dermatitis in herbal formulas (for example NCT02539277, NCT05455060), and cannot isolate its effect.[6][7]

Human trials involving the plant have used it as part of herbal formulas for other conditions. A randomized trial of a Houttuynia-based Chinese herbal formula examined allergic rhinitis symptoms during the COVID-19 pandemic [11]. A Chinese randomized trial of 102 ulcerative colitis patients compared a heartleaf houttuynia herb treatment (21 first-episode patients) with sulfasalazine, and a chronic relapse group with olsalazine versus sulfasalazine [12]. Neither assessed skin appearance.

Heartleaf extract became a recognisable K-beauty ingredient in the 2010s, with toners, ampoules and sheet masks sold under that name [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that the marketing claims of antimicrobial, calming and antioxidant anti-ageing action are sourced to retailer material rather than clinical studies [1]. In Asian food culture the plant also has a long standing as a tea and herb, and its traditional use against respiratory complaints led to Chinese research on it during the SARS outbreak [1][3].

timeline.event: China suspends intravenous use of Houttuynia injections after severe reactions.[2]

card.summary: Fish mint extract ("heartleaf") in K-beauty toners; cell data are encouraging, human skin trials are essentially absent.
card.note: Injected forms caused severe reactions; patch-test advice for topical use.

quick.overview:
Houttuynia cordata is a herb eaten in East and Southeast Asia and used in traditional medicine. Its extract, "heartleaf", is common in Korean skincare marketed for calming redness and oil.

Support comes mainly from cell studies and a small reported toner study; no controlled skin trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids such as quercitrin are reported in cell studies to lower inflammatory mediators and offer antioxidant effects, with antibacterial activity against acne bacteria in vitro.
quick.risks: Contact dermatitis is reported in sensitive users. Injectable forms have caused severe allergic reactions, and high oral doses were toxic in animal studies.

chain: Extract applied in toner, serum or mask
Flavonoids and oils reported to lower inflammatory mediators and microbes in lab studies
Less visible redness and oil, clearer-looking skin
angle.text: Heartleaf toners and sheet masks are used by people with red, oily or breakout-prone skin who want a calmer, clearer look. The claimed route is anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity of the plant's flavonoids and volatile oils.
